title: Cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ by a simple one-axis stretch

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ by a simple one-axis stretch

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The cannon-bones of the ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only in relative length and breadth: at equal length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: (x, y) \mapsto (x, cy): at equal length c \approx 2/3 (sheep), c \approx 1/3 (giraffe) relative to ox

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In other words, the main (and perhaps the only) difference between the two bones is simply that that of the sheep is elongated, along the vertical axis, as compared with that of the ox in the relation of 3/2.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Ungulate cannon-bones and feet”. Scope: metapodial (cannon) bones of ruminant ungulates

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: (x, y) \mapsto (x, cy): at equal length c \approx 2/3 (sheep), c \approx 1/3 (giraffe) relative to ox

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch17-06: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The taxa, ratios and transformation are explicit, and suitable public scans can be analyzed in days. Replicated geometric morphometrics can clearly confirm approximate one-axis scaling or reveal additional shape differences.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Landmark or surface-register ox, sheep and giraffe metapodials, normalize length, and test the stated breadth ratios and whether one-axis affine stretch leaves negligible residual shape differences.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The phrase “essentially only” needs a residual-error threshold.

Age, sex and choice of metapodial affect dimensions.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claimed ratios are numerical and the bones are ordinary museum objects with scans and photographs available. A one-axis scaling leaves a residual that can be tested directly against a more complex shape difference. Within-species variation is the main caveat, and it is measurable in the same specimens.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Scale ox, sheep and giraffe cannon bones to equal length and compare breadth, then inspect residual shape after a single transverse stretch. The claim is confirmed if sheep breadth is about two-thirds and giraffe breadth about one-third of the ox, with little residual shape difference; substantially different ratios, or large residuals at the ends and shaft, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Breed, sex and age change metapodial proportions within domestic ox and sheep.

Giraffe samples in open archives are smaller than livestock samples.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.68
analysis feasibility: 0.76
operationalizability: 0.88
discriminating power: 0.76
data adequacy: 0.62

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: The cannon-bones (fused metacarpal III+IV, and likewise metatarsal) of ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only by a one-axis stretch: scaled to equal greatest length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's, and the residual shape difference after that single transverse scaling is small.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: fetch.py runs the pre-registered catalogue searches and records the URL, time, HTTP status, response size, SHA-256 and hit count of each (derived/source_probe.json). Two further sources were probed with a headless Chrome browser because they return bot challenges to plain HTTP clients: the Archaeology Data Service archive page for the Animal Bone Metrical Archive Project (HTTP 403, Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' interstitial) and Open Context (Anubis challenge page, and a dropped connection from a plain client). No measurement file was downloaded, so there is nothing to analyse and no analysis.py.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using public osteometric measurements of adult metacarpals (greatest length GL and distal breadth Bd, or the same pair of dimensions however the source names them), with at least 10 specimens for ox (Bos taurus) and sheep (Ovis aries) and at least 3 for giraffe (Giraffa): the species median of Bd/GL, expressed relative to the ox, is 0.67 +/- 0.10 for sheep and 0.33 +/- 0.10 for giraffe. If 3D surface meshes rather than tables are used, GL is the maximum caliper length and Bd the maximum extent perpendicular to the long axis within the distal 15% of the bone, both computed from the mesh.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered (claim refuted). Either relative breadth ratio falls outside its stated window, or (where a second breadth, e.g. mid-shaft, is available) the two breadth ratios for the same species differ by more than 0.15, which would mean a single transverse scaling does not describe the difference. If the measurements for any of the three species cannot be obtained from public sources without authentication, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: metacarpal distal breadth / greatest length, relative to ox

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's Fig. 346 compares the three cannon-bones drawn to the same length, so the operational quantity is breadth at equal length, i.e. the ratio Bd/GL, and the claim is about the ratio of that quantity between species (sheep/ox = 2/3, giraffe/ox = 1/3). The +/- 0.10 windows come from the within-species spread of metapodial proportions reported in zooarchaeology (breed, sex and age change Bd/GL by a few percent, not by tens of percent). Metacarpals are used because they are what Thompson figures; metatarsals would serve equally if the same three species are measured the same way. Candidate sources, to be queried in this order: MorphoSource (3D meshes), the Animal Bone Metrical Archive Project and other zooarchaeological osteometric archives (ox and sheep), Open Context zooarchaeology, FuTRES/GEOME trait records, and Zenodo/Dryad datasets. No measurements have been inspected before this pre-registration; only hit counts and HTTP status codes from catalogue searches.

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
No public source was found that gives cannon-bone greatest length and breadth, or a measurable 3D mesh, for all three of ox, sheep and giraffe. Ox metacarpal meshes exist on MorphoSource (5 laser scans) but sheep metacarpals return nothing there and the only giraffe media is a cranium; the single Dryad giraffe limb-bone dataset is 8.5 GB of CT imagery of metatarsals with no comparative material.

The two large zooarchaeological osteometric archives that would supply ox and sheep (the Animal Bone Metrical Archive Project at the Archaeology Data Service, and Open Context) are behind bot challenges (Cloudflare 403 and Anubis) that a headless browser did not clear in this run; even if cleared, neither contains giraffe, so the giraffe third of the claim would still be missing.

The claim is not untestable in principle: measurements of a handful of museum metapodials of the three species, or scans of them, would settle it quickly. The gap is that such measurements are not published as open data. The assessors scored 'data-existence' 0.68-0.86 largely on the expectation that MorphoSource covers ungulate metapodials; for sheep and giraffe it does not.

Hit counts in the probe log are as of 2026-10-31 and will change as catalogues grow; the Zenodo 'giraffe metacarpal' query reports 119 hits only because the terms are OR-combined across full text, and its top results are unrelated.
